After a quick Google search I have found a bug report from 2012 on bugzila - bug no.106 (http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=106)

Does anyone know whether this error message has been caused by me doing something wrong, or is it an actual bug?  If it is, is there a way to fix it?

Thanks in advance

Matt

messages.subject: Covariate-level density estimates with MCDS
messages.body_plain:
I recently read Ronconi et al. 2009 (Aquatic Biology) and Marques et al. 2007 (The Auk) and am interested in using a similar approach for some of my own data. I have line distance sampling data for a shorebird species and I would like to obtain density estimates for habitat type (3 types) and distance from the coast (either within or without 2 km buffer from the coast- binary). I don’t have enough observations to treat habitat type or distance from coast as stratum, therefore I would like to incorporate them into the detection function as observation-level factor covariates using MCDS. However, when I run this analysis, I am able to see the three separate detection functions by habitat type, but I only get a global density estimate in my output. The only way I’ve been able to calculate habitat-level density estimates is to post-stratify by habitat type. Is this the correct approach? I've read through the Distance Sampling books and the online manual.

Any help/advice you may have would be greatly appreciated. I’ve attached a subset of my data for your convenience.

Anne

messages.body_plain:
Yes Anne, post-stratification by habitat type is correct.  Then in the estimate tab of the model definition, request density estimates at both global and stratum resolution, and the same for detection function.  (Encounter rate and cluster size if relevant should be estimated at the stratum level only.)  By specifying detection function at both levels, it tells Distance to fit an mcds model to data pooled across strata, and use the fitted model to estimate mean detectability by stratum according to covariate values for that stratum.

Steve Buckland

good news:  The species filter works fine.  I had expected problems with capitalisation of the name of the field on which you are filtering.  But that is not the case.  Either of the two that follow work fine for your project, resulting in the proper number (160) detections of this species:

bad news:  Distance reports that there are too many point transects in your project: note this summary at the beginning of the results:
 Effort        :    689.0000

 Width         :    75.00000
 # observations:   160

You see the correct number of sightings reported, and even the correct maximum detection distance.  What is incorrect is the number of transects (called samples in the output).  This will of course lead to an incorrect estimate of density.  The cause of this error is your sorting of data by species before importing the data. The data set up needs to respect the survey design, in other words the data are organised according the design rather than according to what was seen during the survey.  If you desire an estimate for each month of the study, then I suggest you construct month*year as strata (all of the same size 774ha), point transects within strata as samples, and species in the observation layer as you have.  Sort your data by strata and points within strata.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate-level density estimates with MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Anne,

(a follow up to Steve's answer re your question)

There is something you must be careful about when implementing this analysis. From your wording, it seems like habitat was an observation level covariate. By selecting it for post-stratification, Distance will associate all the survey effort (i.e. across all habitats) to each habitat stratum. This would make sense e.g. if each post strata is say a class of animal (say males and females), and then you sum up the densities across the strata (which geographically cover the same area) to get the total density.

Here you will have the full effort associated with each stratum, but for each stratum you would want only to account for the effort in that stratum. So densities for each habitat will be biased low, because essentially they will be a weighted average of the density Dx in habitat x and 0 on the other habitats (for which effort is accounted, but no detections are recorded). Therefore, it seems like you would have to increase the obtained density estimates for habitat x by total area/area of habitat x. Of course if you do not know the area of habitat x this might be complicated, but you could try to estimate it.

Note that for this to work coverage must have been uniform over the total area, if some habitats were over or under sampled compared to others this will break apart. If that is the case and you happen to have habitat information at say transect level you might be better off considering explicitly geographic strata (for which you can explicitly define effort and area for each stratum) and still use an MCDS model with habitat as a covariate (and eventually other covariates) considering a pooled detection function with detectability estimates by strata conditional on observed covariate values.

cheers

Tiago

messages.subject: separation of transects
messages.body_plain: Hi.  We estimate density of kangaroos in a number of small nature reserves (1.4 to 20 sq km). Based on initial surveys, we calculated the need for 44 km of transects to get a CV of 15%. When 44 km of transect is laid out in the smaller reserves the transects are very close together, down to 35 m apart. Of course we walk nearby transects on different days but my question is whether there is a minimum separation between transects below which it becomes better to repeat fewer transects, analysing the repeats as such (non-independent). Our species of kangaroo (Eastern Grey) is sedentary and it is possible to see large groups in the same spot at the same time day after day so transects a few metres apart would record much the same on different days.  I could not find any guidance in the Distance books on this and wondered if Effective Strip Width (usually around 100 m either side of the transect in our case) was a reasonable minimum for transect separation, below which the same transect should be repeated if necessary to reach the desired number of detections.

Don:

The delay in response is because I don't have any strong guidance to offer on this.  I presume your effort calculations are based upon the equations found in Section 7.2.2 of Buckland et al. (2001).    I bring this up because those equations use a conservative value for "q" of 3.0 in Eqn. 7.1; unless you have computed your own value of q using Eqn 7.2.

There is some discussion of this subject (although it might not be directly related to your issue) in Section 7.8.3 where the issue of repeating transects for purpose of temporal inference, is discussed.

Finally, the advice on survey effort is only a guide and should be tempered by common sense, as you are doing.  Reserves as small as 1.4km^2 can undoubtedly be sampled with less effort than your larger reserves.

I have no adverse reaction to your suggestion about using ESW as an approximate minimum separation distance.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Bootstrap data
messages.body_plain:
Nicholai:

You are looking for the "decryption" of the contents of what Distance calls the "MCDS Engine Bootstrap file".  On p.322 of the Users Guide to Distance 6.2, you will see the passage:

"This file has the same format as the MCDS Engine Stats File, but contains one set of stats records for each bootstrap. These records are appended one after another as the bootstrap progresses"

Following that advice, you can turn back to page 329 of the Users Guide to find 2 tables that describes the organisation of the output in this file.

There is some old R code in the Technical report I wrote found at http://eprints.st-andrews.ac.uk/archive/00000447/  that contains a function called "read.stats.file()"  Most of that code is nearly 10 years old, so could probably be updated, but it might give you a starting point on your journey.
